summary: Sets the rules for extending the NFSv4 family. It covers creating minor versions, adding optional features to existing minor versions, and fixing flaws in published features. These rules supersede earlier minor versioning rules, including those in RFC 5661, and it updates RFC 5661 and RFC 7862.

plainLanguage.summary: A rule book for how a file-sharing system can grow new features without breaking old ones.

questions: what is xdr extension in nfsv4
subtitle: How the NFSv4 file protocol can grow through extensions, corrections and new minor versions without breaking old clients.

tldr.problem: NFSv4 needed to evolve, but earlier every change meant a whole new minor version, and the minor versioning rules were scattered and sometimes modified ad hoc in each minor version document.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC consolidates the rules. Compatible XDR extensions, such as new operations or attributes, may be added to an existing minor version as optional features. Changes that are not compatible require a new minor version. Flaws are fixed by adding a corrected alternative beside the old feature.
tldr.outcome: These rules supersede the minor versioning rules in RFC 5661 and other minor version RFCs, and the RFC updates RFC 5661 and RFC 7862. It requires no IANA actions.

today: RFC 8178 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5661 and RFC 7862. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the rule set for extending NFSv4.

sections.title: Why NFSv4 Needs Extension Rules
sections.content:
NFSv4 is the fourth version of the Network File System protocol. It was built to evolve through new protocol versions, including minor versions, and through certain kinds of modification of existing minor versions.

Previously, every protocol change was part of a new minor version. The client states the minor version in each COMPOUND request, and the server states it in each CB_COMPOUND callback. RFC 8178 says a new minor version is no longer the only route: optional features can be added as extensions, and protocol corrections can be specified inside a single minor version.

The goal is more implementation flexibility while keeping interoperability when the protocol is upgraded. A client and server may each choose a subset of extensions, and both can use the subset they share.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of printing a whole new rule book every time something changes, the club can now stick in extra pages that old members can simply ignore.

sections.title: Versions, Variants and Feature Statuses
sections.content:
The RFC uses "version" for any valid protocol variant built by its rules, and "minor version" only when it means a minor version. A feature package is a set of features defined together, either as part of a minor version or as part of the same extension.

A minor version can have several variants: the base specification combined with any subset of the extension documents published as Proposed Standards, and each set of published corrections. Two variants have names. The base minor version is the minor version as originally defined, and the current minor version includes all extensions and corrections made by Standards Track documents up to that time.

For feature status, the RFC uses OPTIONAL, REQUIRED and the phrase "mandatory to not implement". It will not use RECOMMENDED as a feature status, because that use is inconsistent with RFC 2119 and RFC 8174. The RFC also explains that its guidance to RFC authors is stated without the capitalized keywords, even though it must be followed.
sections.plainLanguage: A game can have the basic rules plus some optional extra cards. Everyone plays with the basic rules, and each group picks which extra cards to add.

sections.title: The XDR Extension Approach
sections.content:
NFSv4 messages are described with XDR. Between major NFS versions, one XDR description was replaced by another. NFSv4 instead extends the XDR in a way that keeps every previously valid message meaning the same thing. A valid extension must satisfy three conditions:

  • the set of valid messages is a superset of the base set;
  • each base message has exactly the same structure and interpretation;
  • each new message is recognized, using the base definition, as part of an unknown extension.

The allowed extensions are adding new operation codes within COMPOUND and CB_COMPOUND, adding new attributes, adding new values to existing enums, adding unassigned bit values to a flag word, and adding new cases to switches that had no default case. New RPC procedures are not allowed.

Not allowed: any other change to the structure of existing requests or replies, adding RPC procedures, and deleting or reusing existing procedures, operation codes, enum values, flag bits or switch cases. An item may be defined as causing an error, as long as the XDR is unaffected.

XDR structures may also overlay nominally opaque fields. Such additions can be made outside the extension framework if they follow the rules set when the opaque fields were added.
sections.plainLanguage: You may add new doors to a house, but you may not move or wall off the old ones. People who only know the old doors can still get around.

sections.title: Knowing and Supporting Protocol Elements
sections.content:
A responder handles a protocol element in one of three ways: it is unknown (not part of its variant), known but not supported, or known and supported. Each has its own family of error codes, for example NFS4ERR_OP_ILLEGAL for an unknown operation and NFS4ERR_NOTSUPP for a known but unsupported one.

Elements in the base minor version are required to be known, and an element required to be known stays required in later minor versions unless a minor version makes it mandatory to not implement. An element added by an extension need not be known in that minor version, but must be known by the next. If a responder knows one element of a feature package, it must know all of them.

A requester can test knowledge by sending a request and reading the error. For example, a GETATTR that returns NFS4ERR_INVAL for an attribute means the attribute is unknown, while NFS4ERR_ATTRNOTSUPP means it is known. The result stays valid as long as the clientid stays valid, and the RFC suggests clients decide on the common variant before acting on user requests.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask a stranger for a word in a language and they say "I don't know that language", that is different from "I know it, but I can't do that". The protocol uses different answers for each so you can tell them apart.

sections.title: Extending an Existing Minor Version
sections.content:
Extensions to the most recently published minor version can be made by publishing the extension as a Proposed Standard, unless that minor version is defined as non-extensible. The extension need not use the Updates header for the RFC that defines the minor version, which remains a valid description of the base variant.

Beyond the XDR rules, there are two further conditions. New callbacks or extended callback XDR may be used only after the server can determine from the client's actions that the client knows about them. Extensions to the structure of responses to existing operations may be sent only if the server can determine that the client is aware of them.

Extension authors may also define a new attribute that tells clients whether the feature is present and supported. Such support can be checked through the supported_attrs attribute, which is convenient when a feature has several new elements.

Adding REQUIRED features, changing the status of existing features, and anything that breaks these rules cannot be done as an extension and needs a new minor version.
sections.plainLanguage: You can pass out new optional worksheets in the middle of the school year, but only to students who have shown they know how to use them.

sections.title: Minor Version Compatibility
sections.content:
Each clientid is devoted to a single minor version. A server that sees a COMPOUND with an inappropriate minor version MUST reject it, and may return either NFS4ERR_BAD_CLIENTID or NFS4RR_MINOR_VERS_MISMATCH (spelled that way in the RFC text). Servers MUST keep the set of supported features and protocol elements unchanged within that context.

To keep clients and servers of different minor versions working together, servers supporting a minor version should support the earlier ones, and clients should react to a minor version mismatch by searching for a lower minor version the server will accept. When a request uses something not known in the requested minor version, the server acts like a server with the smaller XDR would:

  • an unknown operation gets NFS4ERR_OP_ILLEGAL;
  • an unknown attribute gets NFS4ERR_INVAL;
  • an unknown switch case gets NFS4ERR_BADXDR;
  • an unknown flag bit gets NFS4ERR_INVAL.
sections.plainLanguage: A new teacher who is asked about last year's lesson plan must answer using last year's rules, and not mention things that were not in that plan.

sections.title: Correcting Flaws in Published Features
sections.content:
Flaws may be found after a feature or minor version becomes a Proposed Standard. Corrections are best published in a document that obsoletes or updates the defining RFC. Often no XDR change is needed, and a document that simply updates the earlier one is enough. Incompatible behavior changes should not be mandated just to avoid XDR changes.

When XDR changes are needed, existing structures may not be modified or deleted. The correction is added as an extension, so the old and corrected versions act like two independent OPTIONAL features. If the corrected feature fixes a REQUIRED one, the old version stays REQUIRED, while the corrected version is optional but intended to be adopted. The RFC says it should not be described as RECOMMENDED.

This gives several kinds of clients and servers: those that know only the old version, only the new one, or both. Servers supporting both interoperate with every client. In a later minor version, the uncorrected version might become optional or mandatory to not implement, though the RFC thinks the latter unlikely for a considerable time.
sections.plainLanguage: If a recipe has a mistake, you add a corrected recipe card next to it instead of tearing out the old one, so cooks who still use the old card are not lost.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The RFC proposes no substantive protocol changes, so it states that no security considerations apply. It also requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a rule book, not a new machine, so it adds nothing new that could be unsafe.
